title: Understanding the Benefits of Scaffolds through Computational Separations
authors: Jingchu Gai, Adam Block, Andrej Risteski
lab: Carnegie Mellon University (Gai, Risteski) and Columbia University (Block)
date: 19 October 2026 (arXiv v1, the only version as of 26 October 2026)
run_label: run the BFS harness against a fixed-depth reader
code_note: The paper links no code, traces or checkpoints (checked 26 October 2026). Its figures ship as vector PDFs in the arXiv source, which is where every number on this page that is not printed in the text comes from (decode_figs.py)
takeaway: On Branching with Qwen3-1.7B, same-size students trained on a multi-call harness's traces trailed the harness at the same tree by 5 to 16 points on trees of 13 to 40 calls (single runs; within noise on trees of up to 7 calls), and a 4B student matched its teacher; a theorem shows that a breadth-first-search harness over trivial edge lookups decides a problem no fixed-depth transformer with a short chain of thought can if NL is not in TC⁰, a class that excludes the long-trace students the experiments train.
verdict: Believe the measured direction: same-size students trained on these traces fell short, and larger students or simpler harnesses closed the gap (single runs; the gaps at the larger trees are 5 to 16 points, at the smallest within noise). Read the theorem as a clean result about students with a logarithmic chain of thought, not as the cause of the measured gaps, because every distilled student in the experiments writes a long trace.

headline.k: the (3,3) tree, 40 calls: harness against the same-size student trained on its traces (the 85-call tree has no student)
headline.d: read from the printed bar labels

headline.k: at most that many constant-depth edge queries let a breadth-first-search harness decide directed reachability, which is NL-complete
student gain from LoRA rank 16 to 64, and to full fine-tuning; a 4B backbone instead scores 41.6% against the teacher's 40.0%
headline.d: the abstract's "2.2 from LoRA rank" is the full fine-tune

resources.t: The Expressive Power of Transformers with Chain of Thought
resources.n: the result this paper leans on: logarithmically many decoding steps add little to a transformer, linearly many reach all regular languages, polynomially many reach exactly P. It is why a student that writes a long trace escapes Theorem 1.

resources.t: Chain of Thought Empowers Transformers to Solve Inherently Serial Problems
resources.by: Li, Liu, Zhou and Ma, ICLR 2024
resources.n: the circuit view of chain of thought: constant-depth transformers sit in AC0 or TC0 depending on precision, and T steps of chain of thought buy T serial steps.

resources.t: The Parallelism Tradeoff: Limitations of Log-Precision Transformers
resources.n: the upper bound used for the student: a fixed-depth, log-precision transformer is a uniform TC0 circuit, so it cannot solve NL-complete problems unless NL is in TC0.

resources.t: A Little Depth Goes a Long Way: The Expressive Power of Log-Depth Transformers
resources.n: the other side of the same coin: a transformer whose depth grows like log n can decide directed reachability, the problem Theorem 1 uses; Lemma 1 borrows its transcript-enumeration argument.
the tree-shaped harness of Section 5: leaves sample answers, internal nodes synthesise one from their children.

resources.t: Taming Imperfect Process Verifiers: A Sampling Perspective on Backtracking (VGB)
resources.n: the backtracking harness of Section 2, with the Metropolis-style retract rule and the learned verifier.

resources.t: Beyond A*: Better Planning with Transformers via Search Dynamics Bootstrapping
resources.n: where the A* trace format (CREATE, CLOSE, PLAN) comes from; its transformers learn search from such traces at larger sizes.

resources.t: Stream of Search (SoS): Learning to Search in Language
resources.n: the optimistic counterpart: a model trained on serialised search traces learns to search inside one rollout.

resources.t: QED-Nano: Teaching a Tiny Model to Prove Hard Theorems
resources.n: the 4B prover of Section 5's second experiment, and its own harness (RSA: 40.0% to 56.9% on IMO-ProofBench at about 22 times the tokens, as this paper quotes it).
the closest related work by the paper's own account: a transformer absorbing its own chain of thought into its weights, provably for sparse parities.

kb.n: the same theme from the other side: a light harness around a base model reaches tasks the post-trained model has stopped reaching.

kb.t: On-Policy or Off-Policy Learning? A Systematic Study of Distillation Dynamics
kb.n: this paper distils with the simplest recipe (supervised fine-tuning on the teacher's traces); that page measures what on-policy distillation changes.
a leaderboard result bought with a large harness; this paper says why such gains need not fold back into the weights.

kb.t: HarnessDev: Can LLMs Create and Evolve Their Own Agent Harness?
kb.n: harnesses written by models; the gains measured there belong to the model-plus-harness pair, as here.

kb.t: RRSI: Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement of Agent Harnesses
kb.n: a search over harnesses rather than over answers.

kb.t: SoL-Pi: Recursively Scaling Auto-Research Loops for Efficient Agent Harness
kb.n: another loop that keeps state across many model calls.

kb.t: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
kb.n: the harness most agents descend from (the paper cites it as Yao et al., 2022).

topics.n: owns scaffold sensitivity (section 1: the score belongs to the model-plus-harness pair) and trajectories as training data (section 6), the practice this paper puts a limit on.
owns distillation: soft and sequence-level targets, off- and on-policy, what makes a good small model.
owns why a chain of thought adds computation (section 1, with the Merrill and Sabharwal results) and parallel sampling, verifiers and search (sections 2 to 5).
the harness map and the Loop lab.
